seo.metaTitle: Remove the PNG Alpha Channel - Free, No Upload
seo.metaDescription: Blend a transparent image onto a white background and save it with no transparency left at all. Free and unlimited, done in your browser with no upload.
seo.longDescription: Flatten transparency onto white blends every pixel of an image with a white background using its own opacity, and sets the alpha of the result to full everywhere, so the saved file carries no transparency at all. The white is fixed — there is no color control on this page — and the canvas keeps its size, which means a transparent logo comes out as a white square. That is exactly what JPG and BMP expect, and it is the safe way to hand a cutout to an application that does not understand alpha. The files never leave your browser.
facts: Runs entirely in your browser: no upload, no server, no signup.
Always white — the fit onto background tool flattens onto a color you pick.
Once flattened, the transparency cannot be restored; keep the original.
No settings: the result appears as soon as the image loads.
Free with no daily limit, no watermark and no account, also for commercial use.
howTo: Drop the transparent image into the source area, or pick a file from your device.
The result appears at once, opaque, with the transparent parts filled white.
Download it as PNG or JPG; both store the flattened result correctly.

faq.q: Can I choose the background color?
faq.a: Not on this page, which always flattens onto white. To put the cutout on a color of your choice, use the fit onto background tool, which places the image on a canvas filled with the color you pick.

faq.q: Why does my transparent logo look like a white square?
faq.a: Because the transparent area is now filled, and the fill is white. A logo that looked right on a dark page will look wrong after this step, so keep the alpha when the file allows it.

faq.q: Do I even need this for a JPG?
faq.a: No, JPEG has no alpha channel, so saving as JPG flattens on its own. The step matters when the file has to stay a PNG but must not carry transparency, as in some print workflows.

faq.q: Can I get the transparency back afterwards?
faq.a: No. Once the alpha channel is gone that information is not in the file any more, so run the flattening again from the original transparent source rather than from the flattened copy.
